definition: The top number in a blood pressure reading: the pressure in your arteries when the heart contracts and pushes blood out, measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). From middle age onward it is usually the more important of the two numbers for predicting heart attack and stroke.
The bottom number in a blood pressure reading: the pressure in your arteries while the heart relaxes and refills between beats. In a reading of 120/80 mm Hg, it is the 80.

The medical term for blood pressure that stays high over time. The WHO diagnoses it at 140/90 mm Hg or above; US guidelines start at 130/80. It rarely causes symptoms but steadily damages the arteries, heart, brain and kidneys, which is why getting it measured matters.

Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called bad cholesterol. LDL particles carry cholesterol to your tissues, and when there are too many they lodge in artery walls and build up as plaque. Lowering LDL, through diet, exercise or medication, lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke.

High-density lipoprotein cholesterol, nicknamed good cholesterol because HDL particles carry cholesterol away from the arteries and back to the liver. Higher levels are linked with lower heart risk, but drugs that raise HDL have not prevented heart attacks, so it is a marker more than a target.

The most common type of fat in your blood and in your body's fat stores. Levels rise after meals and with excess calories, sugar and alcohol. A fasting level below 150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) is considered normal; high levels add to cardiovascular risk, and very high levels can inflame the pancreas.

A blood test that measures total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides. Also called a lipid profile or cholesterol test, it is one of the main inputs doctors use, along with age, blood pressure and smoking, to estimate your risk of heart attack and stroke.

The slow buildup of fatty, cholesterol-rich plaque inside artery walls, which narrows and stiffens them. It develops silently over decades. If a plaque ruptures, a clot can form and block the artery, causing a heart attack or stroke.

A class of medicines, including atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, that lower LDL cholesterol by reducing how much the liver makes. Large trials show they cut the risk of heart attack and stroke in people at raised risk. Muscle aches are the best-known side effect; serious problems are rare.

The number of times your heart beats per minute when you are awake, calm and still. For most adults it sits between 60 and 100; fit people often run lower because a stronger heart moves more blood with each beat. A resting rate that climbs over time can be an early sign that something is off.

The tiny beat-to-beat variation in the time between heartbeats, often shortened to HRV and tracked by many wearables. Higher variability generally reflects a relaxed, well-recovered nervous system; it drops with stress, illness, alcohol and poor sleep. Your own trend matters more than comparisons with other people.

A common heart rhythm problem in which the upper chambers quiver chaotically instead of beating in an orderly way, making the pulse irregular and often fast. Some people feel palpitations; others feel nothing. Because blood can pool and clot in the heart, it raises the risk of stroke about fivefold.

The medical term for a heart attack. It happens when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, usually by a clot on a ruptured plaque in a coronary artery, and the starved muscle begins to die. Chest pressure, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, breathlessness or a cold sweat mean calling your local emergency number.
